title: Cache key hygiene and tenant microsegmentation review with BlueHarbor Systems
summary: Deep dive on prefix/prompt cache key design, multi-tenant microsegmentation, and safe eviction/quantization tradeoffs for an on-prem/VPC pilot. Agreed to run a 2-week benchmark with conservative keying + namespace isolation, share benchmark harness, and follow up with security docs and pilot runbook.
topics: quantization impact on latency vs accuracy
action_items: Jordan Park - share benchmark harness + load script - due 2026-07-20
Maya Chen - propose keying patterns (3 variants) and expected hit-rate sims - due 2026-07-22
Marisol Vega - send SOC2/KMS attestation questions and SSO metadata - due 2026-07-21
Priya Singh - provide traffic sample and tenant cardinality data export - due 2026-07-19
next_steps: Redwood to provision a dedicated pilot cluster (VPC-connected) and run 2-week benchmark

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-15 11:00 PT / 14:00 ET / 15:00 UTC. Duration: 58m. Recording ID: fh-20260715-001.
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood Solutions), Alex Rivera (BlueHarbor, Dir ML Platform), Priya Singh (BlueHarbor SRE), Tom Gleason (CTO), Marisol Vega (Security).

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — run through current cache key approach at BlueHarbor, look at multi-tenant microsegmentation options, eviction and TTL policies, and then quantization implications for latency/quality. Maya will go into the runtime sketches.

[00:22] Alex: Yeah thanks, Jordan. We've had a few incidents where shared prefix keys caused noisy neighbour latency spikes. We want to avoid a global shared K V cash, uh, KV cache design that leaks across tenants, and also avoid too many misses because our latency SLO is 150 ms p50.

[00:38] Maya: Totally, thanks. Quick clarifying q: when you say "shared" are you referring to a single global namespace or a shared physical cache with logical tenant keys?

[00:45] Tom: Both, I think. Ops initially provisioned a single Redis-like cache with tenant_id prefixed keys. We saw collisions and eviction storms.

[00:55] Priya: And most of our load is short chat sessions — prefix-heavy. So hit-rate matters. But we also have big tenants with high QPS that can thrash the cache.

[01:10] Maya: OK, so there are two objectives: maximize overall hit-rate (to save tokens and reduce runtime work) and guarantee tenant isolation so one noisy tenant doesn't evict hot entries for others. We'll sketch three approaches.

[01:25] Maya: Option A: namespace-per-tenant. Simple: partition keys by tenant namespace + local eviction. Pros: strong isolation, easy to reason about. Cons: small tenants get cold caches and fragmentation, higher memory footprint overall.

[01:45] Alex: That was our naive config. It prevented cross-tenant eviction but our memory usage doubled because each namespace had to hold its own hotset.

[01:55] Maya: Option B: shared cache with tenant-aware consistent hashing. We hash (tenant_id, prompt_fingerprint) to fixed shards. Pros: balances memory use and keeps a tenant's keys co-located, reduces wide-key collisions. Cons: requires shard rebalancing on scaling and you still need admission controls so a tenant can't hog shards.

[02:18] Liam: We recommend adding a per-tenant quota and token-bucket admission at request ingress so the kernel can't be overloaded.

[02:25] Alex: What's the impact on latency if we do shard routing? Extra network hop?

[02:32] Maya: Practically negligible if shard routing is in-process (consistent-hash table) and routing table cached. Extra 0.5–2 ms typical; but can add complexity.

[02:45] Priya: Option C?

[02:47] Maya: Hybrid: hotset fast-path in a small per-tenant pin cache and a larger shared coldset. Eviction: keep LRU in pin cache per tenant; shared layer uses frequency-based eviction. Benefit: small tenants get fast hot hits, big tenants use shared layer. Complexity: need admission policy and careful metrics for hotness and promotion.

[03:15] Tom: Sounds promising. How do you define the cache key itself? We currently do session_id + normalized prompt text. We've had issues with prompt paraphrases creating new keys.

[03:30] Maya: Key hygiene is critical. We propose a 3-component key: tenant_id | prompt_fingerprint | context_signature. Prompt fingerprint is a stable hash of normalized tokenization rather than raw text (strip punctuation, normalize quotes, canonicalize dates). Context signature is a short fingerprint of preceding K tokens in the session if you want to enable prefix caching rather than full prompt dedupe.

[03:55] Alex: Prefix caching for us is important because we often have repeated system prompts + small user variations. But we worry about fingerprint collisions and privacy — could keys leak PII?

[04:10] Marisol: Security note: keys must not contain raw PII. Use hashed fingerprints and rotate HMAC secrets. Also encrypt cache at rest and ensure KMS wraps keys. We need audit logs for cache key access.

[04:30] Jordan: Good call. Redwood also recommends deterministic HMAC over the normalized prompt with per-tenant salt. That way keys are stable but non-reversible.

[04:45] Priya: On eviction storms — we saw periods where a tenant launching a batch of inference jobs flushed shared cache. Any mitigations?

[04:55] Maya: Several: 1) per-tenant admission controls and soft quotas; 2) staggered background prefetch so we don't warm whole hotset at once; 3) write-through vs write-around tradeoffs — we tend to favor write-through for hot prefixes so hits are accurate; and 4) proactive warming for critical paths with rate-limited prefetch.

[05:20] Liam: Also consider bounded pinned memory per-tenant. If tenant exceeds pinned budget, the system demotes items to shared layer instead of evicting other tenants' pinned items.

[05:35] Alex: How about metrics — what should we monitor to trust isolation?

[05:40] Maya: Per-shard and per-tenant: hit-rate, miss-rate, eviction-rate, promoted/demoted counts, tail latency (p95/p99), and cache size per tenant. We also recommend synthetic replay tests to validate eviction under load.

[06:00] Tom: Now quantization — we plan to run 8-bit and try 4-bit on dedicated hardware. Does quantization change the caching strategy?

[06:10] Maya: It does in subtle ways. Quantization reduces per-token latency on GPU but can affect deterministic generation slightly. For cache, saved tokens are same cost-savings regardless, but mismatch risk rises if you rely on exact kv cache binary compatibility across quantized model variants. If you have multiple model variants (float16, int8, int4), cached KV blobs may not be compatible across them.

[06:35] Jordan: Redwood runtime supports compatible KV serialization per model family, but across quantization levels you should treat caches as variant-specific or provide a normalized prefix-to-embedding layer that is quantization-agnostic.

[06:48] Priya: So we need to decide: single model variant for pilot or allow fallback to cheaper quantized variant with cache invalidation?

[06:56] Maya: For pilot we suggest sticking to one model variant to avoid cross-variant invalidation complexity, unless you invest in conversion layers. If you must fallback, mark cached items with model_variant metadata and invalidate on mismatch. That adds storage and lookup complexity.

[07:15] Alex: What about batching? Our peak QPS receives many small requests; batching could help but adds latency complexity.

[07:24] Liam: Redwood's continuous batching tries to balance latency SLO vs throughput. If cache hit occurs, batching not needed because you avoid the model step. But cache miss paths can be batched aggressively in dedicated mode. For low-latency tokens (p50 150 ms) set batching max-wait to 12 ms and prioritize small batches; tune by observed sequence length.

[07:45] Tom: VPC/on-prem constraints: we need audit logs, HSM/KMS integration, and the ability to run inference in our VPC with Redis instances. Is Redwood Private mandatory?

[07:56] Jordan: Not mandatory for pilot. We can run a VPC-connected Redwood Dedicated cluster that peers with your VPC. For full on-prem we'd do Private deployment. Both support KMS integrations, and audit logs are exported to your SIEM.

[08:10] Marisol: Will the cache keys ever leave our VPC in plain form?

[08:14] Maya: No. Keys should be HMAC'd in your VPC before being sent. On Redwood side we store only the hashed key. We also support envelope encryption tied to your KMS.

[08:25] Priya: Sounds good. Let's talk numbers — hit-rate expectations. With normalized prompt fingerprinting and prefix caching we expect 35–55% hit rates for conversational flows where system prompt + user scaffolding repeats. Does that align with reality?

[08:40] Maya: Yes, in our benchmarks similar workloads saw 40% median hit-rate with a well-tuned fingerprinting and hybrid pin/shared layout. Highly templated flows can go 60–80%.

[08:52] Alex: For pilot success we want p50 latency under 150ms and at least 30% token-savings vs baseline. Agreed?

[08:59] Jordan: Agreed. We'll define exact pass/fail in the benchmark runbook.

[09:05] Priya: One last operational question — key rotation and TTL. If we rotate HMAC keys, do we lose access to old keys?

[09:13] Maya: We recommend key-versioned HMACing. Cache items include key_version metadata; the runtime checks current and previous key versions during lookup to avoid mass invalidation during rotation. Stale entries can be GC'd after grace window.

[09:30] Tom: OK this is helpful. Can you recap pilot plan?

[09:36] Jordan: Sure — high level: 1) BlueHarbor provides 48h anonymized tenant traffic and tenant cardinality. 2) Redwood sets up Dedicated VPC cluster with 1 model variant (int8 or fp16 per tuning) and hybrid cache pattern. 3) Redwood runs 2-week benchmark simulating production traffic, collects hit-rate, latency, and eviction metrics. 4) Post-run review, then decide on microsegmentation or on-prem Private if needed.

[09:58] Alex: Great. And deliverables? Benchmark harness, expected hit-rate sim, security pack, and runbook.

[10:05] Jordan: Yep. We'll send those.

[10:12] Marisol: Please include SOC2 artifacts and our KMS integration checklist.

[10:17] Maya: We'll also propose three keying variants — strict normalization, relaxed-tokenized, and context-signature enabled — and run all three in A/B during the benchmark.

[10:30] Priya: Perfect. We'll upload sample logs and tenant map to the secure share.

[10:38] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the action items.

[10:45] End.
